parts.title: Part 1
parts.context: A student phones a café about a part-time job.
script: Hi. I'm calling about the part-time job advertised in your window.
Great. Can I take your name?
Yuki Tanaka. T, A, N, A, K, A.
Yes, I'm studying chemistry at the university.
When would you be available to work?
On Saturdays and Tuesdays. I don't have lectures on Tuesdays.
Have you worked in a café before?
Not in a café, but I worked in a bakery for a year before university.
That's useful experience. The pay is twelve pounds an hour, and you get a free lunch during your shift.
That sounds good. Is there any training?
Everyone has to complete a one-day food hygiene course before they start. We pay for it.
We provide a T-shirt and an apron, but you'll need to wear black trousers and comfortable shoes.
Would you be able to come in for a trial shift on Friday afternoon?
When you arrive, ask for Maria. M, A, R, I, A. She's the supervisor.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.context: A curator introduces a new exhibition at an art gallery.
script: Good morning, and welcome to the Harbour Gallery. I'm Ingrid, the curator of our new exhibition, The Sea in Art.
The exhibition brings together over two hundred works showing how artists have responded to the sea, from the sixteenth century to the present day.
The most valuable piece in the show is a large seventeenth-century painting of a storm, which has been loaned to us by a museum in Madrid. It's the first time it has left Spain.
You're welcome to take photographs throughout, as long as you don't use flash.
There's a free audio guide, which you can listen to on your own phone by scanning the codes on the walls.
Let me explain the layout. Room one contains early maps of the coastline, some decorated with sea monsters.
Room two is full of detailed ship models, many made by sailors during long voyages.
In room three, you'll find photographs of fishing communities from the nineteen-fifties.
Room four is dark, because it contains a video installation that surrounds you with the sounds and images of waves.
Room five has sculptures made from objects washed up on beaches, including plastic.
And finally, in the garden room, we're showing paintings by local schoolchildren, who were asked what the sea means to them.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.context: Two students, Cara and Musa, plan a study of pedestrians who use phones.
script: Cara, why did you want to study people who use phones while walking?
Last term a friend of mine was hit by a bicycle because she was texting and didn't look. Luckily she wasn't badly hurt, but it made me think.
OK. Where should we observe people?
At the pedestrian crossing near the main campus gate. Hundreds of students use it every hour.
In our pilot study, the main finding was that people using phones took noticeably longer to cross.
Yes, and they were less likely to look both ways. We need to be careful about ethics, though.
We didn't record anyone's face, and we didn't collect names. That should be enough.
What should we recommend at the end?
I like the idea of painted warnings on the pavement, telling people to look up. Some cities have tried that.
Good. Now, ideas for the main study. I think we should observe at different times of day, not just in the morning.
Agreed. I'd suggest using video recording, so we can check our counts later.
But then we'd need permission from everyone. Let's not. I'd also like to interview some pedestrians afterwards, to ask whether they noticed the traffic.
And I'd like to compare our results with data from other countries.
And we both think we should present the final results to the city council.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.context: A lecture on wetlands and climate change.
script: Today I want to talk about wetlands, which are among the most valuable and most threatened ecosystems on Earth.
Wetlands, including marshes, swamps and peatlands, cover only about six percent of the world's land surface. But they play a role in the climate that is far greater than their size suggests.
Peatlands are particularly important. Although they cover only around three percent of the land, they store about twice as much carbon as all the world's forests combined.

Why? In waterlogged soil, there is very little oxygen, so dead plant material is not fully broken down. Decomposition is so slow that the material builds up over thousands of years, locking away carbon.
Coastal wetlands, such as mangroves and salt marshes, are also excellent carbon stores. The carbon they hold is often called blue carbon.

The problem is that when wetlands are drained, usually for farming or building, the stored carbon is released as carbon dioxide. Dried peat also becomes extremely vulnerable to fires. In 2015, peat fires in Indonesia produced a haze that covered large parts of South-East Asia.

Wetlands have other benefits too. They act like sponges, absorbing heavy rain and reducing flooding downstream. They also filter pollutants from water, which is why they are sometimes called the kidneys of the landscape.

International efforts to protect wetlands go back to the Ramsar Convention, signed in 1971. Today, many projects are restoring damaged peatlands by blocking drainage ditches, so that the land becomes wet again.

passages.title: The Humble Potato
paragraphs: Few foods have had as great an impact on world history as the potato. It was first domesticated around 8,000 years ago in the Andes mountains of South America, in the region that is now southern Peru and north-western Bolivia. Andean farmers developed thousands of varieties, adapted to different altitudes and climates, and many are still grown there today.

Andean peoples also developed ingenious ways of preserving potatoes. One of the best known is chuño, a freeze-dried potato made by leaving potatoes outside to freeze during cold mountain nights, then trampling them to remove water and drying them in the sun. Chuño can be stored for years, providing food security in difficult times.

Spanish explorers encountered the potato in the sixteenth century and brought it to Europe around the 1570s. At first, Europeans were suspicious. The plant belongs to the same family as poisonous nightshade, and some people believed that potatoes caused disease. For a long time, they were grown mainly as animal feed or as a curiosity in botanical gardens.

Attitudes changed gradually. In France, the pharmacist Antoine-Augustin Parmentier became one of the potato's greatest champions. He had eaten potatoes as a prisoner of war in Prussia and was impressed by their nutritional value. According to a popular story, he planted a field of potatoes near Paris and placed guards around it during the day, making the crop seem valuable. At night, when the guards left, local people stole the potatoes and began growing them themselves.

By the nineteenth century, potatoes had become a staple food across much of Europe, as they produced far more calories per acre than grain. In Ireland, a large part of the population came to depend almost entirely on them. When a disease called potato blight, caused by a fungus-like organism, arrived in Ireland in 1845, it destroyed crops for several years. Around one million people died, and another million emigrated.

Today, the potato is one of the world's most important food crops, grown in more than 150 countries. China is now the largest producer. Scientists continue to draw on the genetic diversity of Andean varieties to develop potatoes that can resist disease and cope with a changing climate.

passages.title: Learning From Nature
paragraphs: For billions of years, living things have been solving problems: how to stay cool, how to move efficiently, how to stick to surfaces or keep clean. Biomimicry is the practice of studying these solutions and applying them to human design. The term was popularised by the American writer Janine Benyus in her 1997 book on the subject, but people have been borrowing ideas from nature for much longer.

One of the best-known examples began with a walk. In 1941, the Swiss engineer George de Mestral returned from a hike with his dog and noticed burrs, the seed heads of a plant, stuck to his trousers and to the dog's fur. Under a microscope, he saw that the burrs were covered in tiny hooks that caught on loops of fabric. After years of experiments, he developed Velcro, a fastener made of hooks and loops.

In Japan, nature helped solve a problem with high-speed trains. When early Shinkansen trains came out of tunnels at high speed, they produced a loud boom that disturbed people living nearby. An engineer named Eiji Nakatsu, who was also a keen birdwatcher, noticed how the kingfisher dives into water with hardly a splash. The train's nose was redesigned to resemble the bird's long, narrow beak. The new design was quieter, and it also used less electricity.

Architects have also learned from animals. The Eastgate Centre, an office building in Harare, Zimbabwe, was designed to copy the way termites keep their mounds at a stable temperature, using a system of vents and chimneys that allows air to circulate naturally. The building uses far less energy for cooling than conventional buildings of a similar size.

Other examples involve surfaces. The leaves of the lotus plant stay clean because they are covered in tiny bumps and a waxy coating that make water form round droplets, which roll off and carry dirt away. This 'lotus effect' has inspired self-cleaning paints and glass. Researchers have also studied geckos, whose feet are covered in millions of tiny hairs that allow them to climb smooth walls, to develop new adhesives.

However, biomimicry is not automatically environmentally friendly. A product inspired by nature may still be made from harmful materials or use large amounts of energy. Moreover, nature's solutions evolved for particular conditions and cannot always be transferred directly to human problems. The most useful approach, many designers argue, is to treat nature as a source of inspiration rather than a blueprint to be copied exactly.

passages.title: Taking Back the Streets
paragraphs: For much of the twentieth century, cities were redesigned around the car. Roads were widened, parking spaces multiplied and pedestrians were pushed to the edges. In recent decades, however, a growing number of cities have begun to reverse this trend, restricting cars in their centres and giving space back to people.

The Spanish city of Pontevedra was one of the pioneers. In 1999, its new mayor closed most of the historic centre to private cars, allowing only deliveries, residents' access and emergency vehicles. Pavements were widened and streets were turned into public spaces. While many Spanish towns of a similar size have lost population, Pontevedra's centre has attracted new residents and businesses.

More recently, the Norwegian capital, Oslo, removed most of the parking spaces in its central area between 2017 and 2019, replacing them with benches, cycle lanes, small parks and play areas. Many shopkeepers had warned that they would lose customers. In practice, the number of people visiting the centre did not fall, and in my view such fears are often exaggerated, since people on foot and on bicycles tend to visit shops more frequently than drivers.

Larger cities have taken a variety of approaches. In Paris, roads along the banks of the River Seine were turned into pedestrian areas in 2016, and hundreds of kilometres of cycle lanes have been built. Barcelona has created 'superblocks', groups of nine city blocks in which through-traffic is restricted and the inner streets are reclaimed for people.

These changes are not without problems. Disabled people and elderly residents who depend on cars may find it harder to reach the places they need. Businesses still need deliveries, and traffic removed from one area may simply move to surrounding streets, increasing congestion and pollution there. Some delivery companies have responded by using electric cargo bikes for the final part of their journeys.

I believe the evidence shows that reducing the dominance of cars makes cities healthier, safer and more pleasant. But such policies must be designed carefully. Exemptions should be made for disabled people and emergency vehicles, public transport must be improved before cars are restricted, and residents should be involved in decisions from the start. A city designed for people, rather than for cars, is a goal worth pursuing, but it cannot be imposed overnight.

task1.text: The bar chart below shows the average number of hours people in five age groups slept on weekdays and at weekends in one country. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.

chart.title: Average hours of sleep per night

model: The bar chart compares the average amount of sleep that people in five age groups got per night on weekdays and at weekends in one country.

Overall, people in every age group slept longer at weekends than on weekdays, but the difference was much greater for younger people. Among the oldest group, sleep patterns hardly changed between weekdays and weekends.
On weekdays, 18 to 25-year-olds slept the least, at 6.5 hours a night, while people aged 65 and over slept the most, at 7.5 hours. The other three groups slept between 6.8 and 7 hours.

At weekends, teenagers aged 13 to 17 slept for 9.5 hours on average, two and a half hours more than on weekdays, the largest difference of any group. Young adults also slept considerably longer, at 8.5 hours. The gap narrowed with age: people aged 26 to 45 slept one hour more, those aged 46 to 65 only half an hour more, and people over 65 just 0.1 hours more.

task2.text: More and more people are shopping online rather than in traditional shops. Do the advantages of this development outweigh the disadvantages? Write at least 250 words.
model: Online shopping has grown rapidly over the past two decades, and for many people it has become the normal way to buy everything from books to groceries. Although this trend has some serious drawbacks, I believe that, overall, its advantages are greater.

The most obvious benefit is convenience. Customers can shop at any time of day, compare prices across many sellers in seconds and have goods delivered to their door. This is especially valuable for people who live far from shops, work long hours or have limited mobility. Online shopping also offers a much wider range of products than any physical shop, and competition between sellers often keeps prices lower. In addition, small businesses and craftspeople can reach customers across the country or even the world without the cost of renting a shop.

However, there are real disadvantages. As more people shop online, many traditional shops have closed, leaving empty high streets and costing jobs. Town centres can lose their sense of community when people no longer meet in shops and markets. There are also environmental concerns: individual deliveries and large amounts of packaging increase emissions and waste, and the ease of returning items encourages people to buy more than they need. Finally, online shoppers face risks such as fraud and the misuse of personal data.

Many of these problems can be reduced. Town centres can adapt by offering experiences, such as cafés, events and services, that cannot be bought online, and delivery companies can use electric vehicles and shared collection points.
In conclusion, while online shopping has damaged some high streets and has environmental costs, I believe its convenience, choice and opportunities for small businesses outweigh these disadvantages.

speaking.cue:
Describe a time when you worked in a team.
You should say:
- what the task was
- who was in the team
- what your role was
and explain how you felt about working in this team.
speaking.cueModel: I'd like to talk about a startup competition I took part in with three other students from my university. The task was to come up with an idea for a business that could solve a real social or environmental problem, and then present it to a panel of judges. Our idea was an automated rooftop garden that used sensors to water plants and collect rainwater, so that people in cities could grow food with very little effort. There were four of us: two engineering students who built the prototype, a business student who worked on the budget, and me. My role was mainly the software, writing the code that read the sensor data and controlled the watering, and I also helped to design our presentation. It wasn't always easy. We had different working styles, and close to the deadline we argued quite a lot about how much to include in the presentation. But we learned to listen to each other and divide the work according to our strengths. In the end, we reached the final round, which none of us had expected. I really enjoyed it, because I learned that a team can achieve much more than individuals working alone, as long as everyone respects each other's skills.
